reason: Seawater can enter seafloor fractures, starting the circulation toward hot rock.
expectation: I expect mineral-bearing seawater to flow into the fractures, though the exact result is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: The early sea could also enter the fractures, but I chose the water already carrying dissolved minerals.

effect: Seawater has entered the crust, so the next step is to heat it.
reaction: The connection between seafloor fractures and circulation is clear.
reason: This is the only offered combination, and hot rock should heat the infiltrating seawater.
expectation: I expect the seawater to heat up, possibly reacting with the rock.

effect: The seawater is heated and remains confined below the surface; it may now react further with the rock.
reaction: The role of confining pressure is interesting.
reason: This is the only offered combination, and continued contact with hot rock may change the water's chemistry.
expectation: I expect hot water to react with the rock and carry dissolved minerals, though the exact result is uncertain.

effect: The heated water has exchanged dissolved constituents with the rock; it can now follow fractures back toward the sea.
reaction: The dependence of the reactions on local conditions is a useful detail.
reason: This is the only offered combination, and fractures could provide a route for the hydrothermal fluid to rise.
expectation: I expect the mineral-bearing fluid to move upward through the fractures, possibly emerging at the seafloor.

effect: Buoyancy and pressure differences are carrying the heated fluid back toward the sea through fractures.
reaction: The separate entry and return routes make the circulation loop clearer.
reason: Cooler seawater should mix with the rising fluid and may cause dissolved minerals to precipitate.
expectation: I expect the hot fluid to cool on meeting seawater, perhaps forming a mineral deposit.

alternatives.reason: The early sea could also receive the returning fluid, but the cooler seawater seems more directly relevant to vent deposits.

effect: Cooling and mixing have caused minerals to precipitate; the deposit may now build around the fractures.
reaction: It is satisfying to see dissolved material become solid as conditions change.
reason: Combining the precipitating minerals with the fractures seems likely to build the vent deposit.
expectation: I expect a mineral deposit to form around the seafloor vent, though its exact shape is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Returning the hot fluid to the sea should advance the other goal, but I want to follow the precipitation first.

effect: The precipitated minerals built a deposit around the outlet, completing the vent-deposit goal.
reaction: The modest deposit is a useful contrast to assuming every vent forms a tall chimney.
reason: The only offered combination should return the heated fluid to the sea and advance the remaining goal.
expectation: I expect the hot fluid to emerge into the sea, completing the circulation route.

effect: The hot fluid returned to the sea as a hydrothermal plume, completing the circulation goal and the chapter.
reaction: The distinction between suspended minerals and smoke was a useful final detail.

mostWorthwhile.text: Following the heated fluid through fractures and into cooler seawater was most worthwhile: it connected circulation, mixing and mineral precipitation.

leastWorthwhile.text: Heating the water and then combining it with hot rock again felt somewhat repetitive, even though the second step explained chemical exchange.

surprise.text: The plume’s visible material is suspended minerals, not smoke; the deposit also need not be a towering chimney.

arbitrary.text: The first choice between two forms of seawater had no clear practical distinction in the offered options; I chose the mineral-bearing water without knowing whether it mattered.

continue.text: Yes. The concise explanations made the circulation loop understandable, and I would be curious to see another natural process unfold, though the forced sequence offered few meaningful choices.
